quarterly_data.signal: CFO Brian Olsavsky: Q2 worldwide operating income of $27.5 billion includes two items that reduced expenses by approximately $1.2 billion. First, tariff-related refunds of approximately $600 million, included in the North America segment, which represent 'the significant majority of refunds we expect to receive'. Second, a separate benefit of approximately $600 million from the change in fair value measurement of energy contracts subject to derivative accounting, primarily in the AWS segment; these energy contracts are to secure electricity supply for existing and future operations, and changes in their fair value will create unrealized gains and losses within operating expenses. He said the refund amount is limited because Amazon forward-bought and pre-positioned inventory to avoid tariff costs and is not the importer of record for the large majority of items sold in its store; where it can trace specific import charges passed on to customers it will refund those customers, and otherwise it will use the refunds to keep investing in low prices.
quarterly_data.figure: approximately $1.2 billion of expense benefits in Q2: ~$600 million tariff-related refunds (North America) + ~$600 million energy-contract fair-value benefit (primarily AWS)

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Brian Olsavsky on segments: Q2 revenue includes the timing shift of Prime Day into Q2 for most of Amazon's largest countries, including the U.S. North America segment revenue was $116.2 billion, up 16% year over year, with operating income of $9.1 billion and a 7.9% operating margin; International segment revenue was $42.2 billion, up 15% year over year excluding foreign exchange, with operating income of $1.7 billion and a 4.1% operating margin. Worldwide paid units grew 17% year over year, and Prime membership grew double digits year over year.
quarterly_data.figure: North America $116.2 billion (+16% YoY), operating income $9.1 billion (7.9% margin); International $42.2 billion (+15% YoY ex-FX), operating income $1.7 billion (4.1% margin); paid units +17%

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Brian Olsavsky on the Q3 2026 guidance: two factors drive the sequential deceleration in net sales growth from Q2 to Q3 — the Prime Day timing shift (in 2026 the event fell in Q2 for most large countries including the U.S., while in 2025 Prime Day was entirely in Q3) and an unfavorable impact of approximately 80 basis points from year-over-year changes in foreign exchange rates based on current rates. After adjusting for Prime Day, heading into Q3 the stores business sees 'strong customer engagement, growth, and a continuation of the trends that we have seen in the first half of the year'.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 guidance includes an unfavorable foreign-exchange impact of approximately 80 basis points

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Brian Olsavsky on fulfillment: Amazon is expanding its deployment of robotics and automation, retrofitting facilities with its latest-generation technology, and expects to more than double its fleet of robotic arms, like Cardinal and Sparrow, in 2026; the network made progress optimizing inventory placement, shortening shipping distances, reducing touches per package and improving consolidation rates. Amazon faces heightened transportation costs from fuel inflation driven by the conflict in the Middle East and higher line-haul rates from driver capacity limitations; excluding higher fuel and line-haul rates, shipping costs grew more slowly than worldwide unit growth, and the operating-income impact is partially offset by the FBA fuel and logistics surcharge implemented in April. He said operating margin may fluctuate and progress may not always be linear.
quarterly_data.figure: fleet of robotic arms expected to more than double in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: AWS profitability and returns: CFO Brian Olsavsky said 'the profitability you're seeing from AWS isn't random' — it results from disciplined efficiency gains, capacity optimization (which AWS 'benefited quite a bit from in Q2') and closely managing fixed costs — and that AWS margins will fluctuate with investment levels, product mix and the mix of AI versus non-AI; software and process improvements optimize server capacity and build a more efficient network using lower-cost custom silicon and custom network gear. He sees 'a strong linkage between AI spend and core growth' and expects the relationship to strengthen as more AI workloads move into full-scale production. CEO Andy Jassy: 'We see the margins and returns in AI tracking what we saw with Core at the same point of evolution, actually a little ahead', and 'At this level of spend and higher, we have clear line of sight to strong financial returns'; with many data centers being built simultaneously ahead of monetization, Amazon will encounter free cash flow headwinds until they come online, and AWS has a track record of pulling forward break-evens on server equipment and extending its useful life. Jassy said more enterprises are building plans to move from on-premises to the cloud and AWS is 'winning the lion's share of those'.

CEO Andy Jassy on chips: Amazon is 'unusually well-positioned for this AI inflection' with leading price-performance chips in AI (Trainium) and CPU (Graviton); 'We just have an incredible amount of demand for Trainium', and many customers are excited about using it in the form AWS provides today. Amazon also continues 'to have a deep partnership with Nvidia' and will keep making AWS the best place to run NVIDIA chips, because some customers 'will run on Nvidia for as long as we can foresee' and customers want choice, which helps drive the cost of inference down.

CEO Andy Jassy on AWS AI services: Bedrock carries the leading models (Anthropic, OpenAI and open models) and is 'continuing to grow incredibly quickly'; his view is that AWS and Amazon 'can have a wildly successful business without its own frontier model' because no single model will rule the world. Bedrock Agents (managed agent infrastructure) also added a new harness that speeds up how fast customers assemble agents, including creating the agent with Strands. Amazon Q (AI work companion) added in Q2 autonomous background agents set up in plain language, a personalized activity feed and 16 new integrations including Adobe, Moody's and Snowflake; companies using Q include 3M, Allianz, AstraZeneca, Autodesk, BMW, Exxon, FINRA, Hyundai, Intuit, Mondelez International, Moody's, the NBA, the NFL, Sun Life and Southwest Airlines. Amazon Connect (call center service) is used by all five major leading airline providers and many leading banks and healthcare companies and continues to grow very quickly; AWS Transform (software migration) is growing quickly; Jassy expects AWS Continuum 'to grow quickly' and said several more agentic applications are in development.
quarterly_data.figure: Amazon Q: 16 new integrations in Q2

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Andy Jassy on Stores: Amazon added millions of new products, including over 700,000 from notable brands, and expanded ultra-low-price selection on Amazon Haul in the U.S. by nearly 20x since launch (over 6 million items priced under $10); on Prime Day more than 80% of deals were at Amazon's lowest price of the year. Amazon is the second-largest grocer in the U.S., with over $150 billion of gross merchandise sales last year: monthly active perishables customers grew over 50% since the start of the year, same-day orders with perishables average over 3x more units per order, same-day perishables are offered in 2,300 U.S. cities, Whole Foods Market is significantly outpacing the growth of comparable grocers, and the new Daily Shop urban format is expanding very rapidly. Amazon Pharmacy more than doubled its new customers in the first six months, and same-day prescription deliveries grew nearly 5x. Amazon delivered over 40% more items same day or overnight in the first half than a year earlier. Amazon Now (delivery in 30 minutes or less) added 80 U.S. cities and towns and several major cities in Egypt in Q2, is available in nine countries and over 250 cities and towns, saw over 80% quarter-over-quarter growth in sales and units sold and served over 60% more customers quarter over quarter. Amazon recently launched Amazon Supply Chain Services, with large customers including Procter & Gamble, 3M, Lands' End and American Eagle Outfitters.
quarterly_data.figure: grocery over $150 billion gross merchandise sales (last year); over 40% more items delivered same day or overnight (first half); Amazon Now in nine countries and over 250 cities and towns

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Andy Jassy on Ads and devices: Amazon Ads generated $19.8 billion of revenue, up 26% year over year, with Sponsored Products the largest offering and a key growth driver; shoppers who click a sponsored prompt in Amazon's agentic and conversational experiences (Alexa+, Alexa for Shopping) convert to a sale 48% more often and spend 21% more on average; ad inventory on Thursday Night Football, NBA, WNBA and NASCAR all sold out, and Amazon introduced more than 30 new advertisers to the NBA in its first year; advertisers using Ads Agent targeting see 8% lower cost per impression and 6% lower cost per acquisition. Alexa for Shopping (agentic AI shopping assistant) was used by over 350 million customers in the last 12 months, and in Q2 its active users nearly doubled and interactions rose over 5x year over year; Alexa+ expanded to Germany, Austria, France and Brazil. Amazon Leo has more than 20 partners who will extend the reach of its satellite network.
quarterly_data.figure: Ads revenue $19.8 billion (+26% YoY); Alexa for Shopping used by over 350 million customers in the last 12 months
